L2280@P99: In December 1944 an updated version was introduced, designated as the M3A1. It had several
L2281@P99: new features, including a recess machined into the bolt that allowed it to be cocked with the
L2282@P99: user’s finger. The ejection port and ejection port cover were enlarged, a magazine release button
L2283@P99: cover was added and a magazine loading device was welded to the wire stock. In 1945 the
L2284@P99: Guide Lamp factory manufactured 15,500 M3A1 submachine guns, with an additional 33,000
L2285@P99: weapons manufactured by the Ithaca Gun Company during the Korean War. M3 and M3A1
L2286@P99: were officially retired from US service in 1957; however they continued to be used until the
L2287@P99: early 1990s by armored vehicle crews.

L2291@P100: The Browning Automatic Rifle (commonly known as the BAR), was designed in 1917 by John
L2292@P100: M. Browning, as a replacement for French-made light automatic rifles. The BAR was a .30
L2293@P100: caliber, gas-operated, select-fire, air-cooled, automatic rifle that fired from an open bolt fed from
L2294@P100: a 20-round detachable box magazine.
L2295@P100: M1818A2 Browning Automatic Rifle
L2296@P100: The BAR saw little action in WWI, its first action being in September of 1918. In 1922, the
L2297@P100: M1922 BAR was introduced. This version was equipped with a flanged or finned barrel and
L2298@P100: side-mounted sling swivel, and was intended for use by the cavalry. In June 1937, a small
L2299@P100: number of M1918s were modified to include a spiked bipod attached to the gas cylinder and a
L2300@P100: hinged butt plate. These weapons were designated as the M1918A1 Automatic Rifle. In 1940,
L2301@P100: the M1918A2 was introduced. This model was fully automatic fire only. The rate of fire being
L2302@P100: adjustable with a choice between "fast-auto" (500–650 round per minute) and "slow-auto" (300–
L2303@P100: 450 rounds per minute). The bipod was now attached to the barrel and a flash hider was added, a
L2304@P100: rear monopod was hinged to the butt, and the weapon's role was changed to that of a squad
L2305@P100: automatic weapon. In 1942, a fiberglass butt stock replaced the wood version, and late in the
L2306@P100: war, a barrel-mounted carrying handle was added. The BAR continued in use until the late
L2307@P100-101: 1950s. Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2308@P101: Chapter 8 Late – 20th, Early 21st Century 1954-2006
L2309@P101: Part 1 Uniforms
L2310@P101: In 1954 the Army began to make changes to the uniform that it had been
L2311@P101: contemplating since just after the end of World War II. One of the most
L2312@P101: significant factor effecting decisions made about the new uniforms was
L2313@P101: the philosophy embraced by the Army leadership that officers and
L2314@P101: enlisted uniforms should be the same, distinguished only by insignia.
L2315@P101: Although the changes were begun in 1954, it would take until the end of
L2316@P101: the decade before they were fully implemented.
L2317@P101: Army Chief of Staff, General J. Lawton Collins, approved the reintroduction of a dress blue
L2318@P101: uniform for enlisted men. The uniform was not intended for general issue, but was authorized to
L2319@P101: be purchased at the option of the individual. Specifications for the enlisted dress blue coat were
L2320@P101: established in 1956 and matched those of the army green service coat. The trousers were the
L2321@P101: same as those specified for officers in 1953 with a gold stripe on the outer leg seam.
L2322@P101: The Optional Enlisted Man’s
L2323@P101: Dress Blue Uniform
L2324@P101: On September 2, 1954 the adoption of
L2325@P101: the Army Green Uniform in shade 44
L2326@P101: was announced in Circular 102, but it
L2327@P101: was not until September 1956 that it
L2328@P101: became available at Quartermaster
L2329@P101: Clothing Sales Stores, and late 1957
L2330@P101: before issues began to inductees.
L2331@P101: After a transition period to allow
L2332@P101: wear-out of existing uniforms, the
L2333@P101: green uniform became mandatory
L2334@P101: service dress in September 1961.
L2335@P101: The new coat was single breasted
L2336@P101: with four bright brass general service
L2337@P101: buttons in front, a roll collar and
L2338@P101: notched lapels. Bright brass collar
L2339@P101: discs continued to be worn with the
L2340@P101: distinctive unit insignia worn on the
L2341@P101: shoulder loops. The uniform was to
L2342@P101: be worn with a light tan shirt, a black
L2343@P101: four-fold service necktie, black socks,
L2344@P101: black low quarter shoes and an Army
L2345@P101: green service cap with a black visor
L2346@P101: and chinstrap, or the Army green
L2347@P101: garrison cap piped in dark green.
L2348@P101: The Army Green Uniform
L2349@P101: The black accessories were adopted as the result of a Department of Defense Standardization
L2350@P101: Program established by Congress in l954. The change from russet to black was to reduce the
L2351@P101: amount of items in the military supply system by making them the same for all of the services.
L2352@P101-102: 99Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2353@P102: The wool serge shade 44 material used in the Army Green Uniform became an all-season Army
L2354@P102: green shade 344 polyester and wool tropical blend on July 13, 1964, and Army green shade 489
L2355@P102: polyester and wool serge by 1990. The Army tan shade 46 cotton shirt was changed to an Army
L2356@P102: green shade 415 polyester and cotton blend in 1979. This shirt is worn with shoulder marks to
L2357@P102: indicate rank, when not worn under the service coat.

L2366@P102: khaki shade 1, and consisted of a long sleeve
L2367@P102: shirt and trousers worn with low quarter shoes
L2368@P102: and the garrison cap. Combat boots were
L2369@P102: authorized for wear with the khaki uniform by
L2370@P102: airborne troops, military police, color and honor
L2371@P102: guards, and at graduations.
L2372@P102: In 1955 an abbreviated version of the uniform
L2373@P102: was authorized, consisting of a short sleeve
L2374@P102: shirt, shorts, and knee socks with production

L2388@P103: Testing for a durable press tan
L2389@P103: summer uniform began in 1968, but

L2395@P103: drill sergeants began in 1969, and

L2399@P103: However, problems with quality
L2400@P103: control continued to plague

L2406@P103: In 1958 the rank structure was again changed with enlisted grades from E-1 to E-9. The rank of
L2407@P103: Private (E-2) and Command Sergeant Major (E-9) were added in 1968 without a change to the
L2408@P103: basic rank structure. There were specialist badges for each of the grades as well, but most of
L2409@P103: these were eliminated in the 1970s until only Specialist (E-4) remained. In 1979 shoulder marks
L2410@P103: were introduced for wear on the green Class B shirt and the black wool sweater, and in 1998
L2411@P103: same-size male and female chevrons are introduced.

L2419@P104: The Army Uniform Board appointed a special subcommittee on caps in 1950 to develop a cap
L2420@P104: design for the general duty uniform. The committee recommended a solid construction service
L2421@P104: cap in one shade, similar in design to the cap developed by the Quartermaster Corps for the Air
L2422@P104: Force in l948. The Army adopted a modified version of this cap on September 9, 1954. The
L2423@P104: new cap was made of Army Green shade 44 wool serge with a black leather visor and chinstrap.
L2424@P104: It had a straight, high front and relaxed crown, and a bright brass disc with the US Coat of Arms
L2425@P104: was worn centered on the front. The cap was authorized for wear with both the summer khaki
L2426@P104: uniforms as well as with the Army Green Uniform. The same design in dark blue piped in
L2427@P104: yellow was also used for Dress Blue Uniform cap. The committee also decided that the olive
L2428@P104: drab wool and the khaki cotton garrison caps piped in branch colors would be replaced with a
L2429@P104: single pattern of garrison cap in Army green shade 44, wool serge piped in dark green.

L2453@P104-105: 102Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2454@P105: An olive green shade 107, cotton utility uniform was introduced in 1952 gradually replacing the
L2455@P105: herringbone twill (HBT) uniform adopted in World War II. Specifications for the utility jacket
L2456@P105: were dated August 30, 1952, and the matching cotton utility trousers were dated November 21,
L2457@P105: 1952 with production beginning in 1953.
L2458@P105: As a result of negotiations with the North Koreans, the “U.S. ARMY” distinguishing insignia
L2459@P105: was introduced on October 27, 1953 and required to be worn above the left pocket on for both
L2460@P105: the field and utility jackets. Many units had local directives that required a cloth tape with the
L2461@P105: soldier's last name stenciled in black letters. In units where standard operating procedures (SOP)
L2462@P105: required the name tape to be worn above the left pocket, they were worn above the U.S. Army
L2463@P105: tape. Most units SOPs, however, required the name tape to be worn above the right pocket,
L2464@P105: which eventually became codified in regulation.
L2465@P105: The Name Tape as authorized by unit SOP The U.S. Army Distinctive Insignia
L2466@P105: An olive green shade107 cotton sateen shirt replaced the utility jacket under specifications dated
L2467@P105: April 12, 1963. The pockets were moved and the pocket flaps now had clipped corners. As a
L2468@P105: result of early experiences in Vietnam, these specifications were again changed again on
L2469@P105: November 6, 1964. The buttons were moved so that the white undershirt was less exposed, the
L2470@P105: pockets now had pointed pocket flaps, and buttoned cuffs were added to the sleeves.
L2471@P105: Left: The durable press utility uniform being worn by
L2472@P105: members of an infantry combat support company in
L2473@P105: 1976. Note the color difference between the between
L2474@P105: the Olive Green shade 507 and Olive Green shade 107
L2475@P105: as seen worn by the Radio Telephone Operator.
L2476@P105: A durable press utility uniform made of olive
L2477@P105: green shade 507, polyester and cotton was
L2478@P105: authorized under specifications dated August
L2479@P105: 25, 1975 which remained in use until replaced
L2480@P105: by the Battle Dress Uniform (BDU) in the mid1980s.
L2481@P105: In 1963, tropical combat clothing was type
L2482@P105: classified for production and issue to soldiers
L2483@P105: serving in Vietnam. There were three basic
L2484@P105: patterns of Tropical Combat Coats. The first
L2485@P105: was made of olive green shade 107, wind
L2486@P105: resistant cotton poplin with two slanted
L2487@P105: bellows-type breast pockets and two bellows
L2488@P105: type lower pockets on the coat. The pockets
L2489@P105: had flaps secured by two exposed plastic
L2490@P105: buttons, an interior button over gas flap,
L2491@P105: shoulder loops, and a double button adjustment
L2492@P105: tab on each side at the waist. The second pattern coat was the basically the same as the first
L2493@P105: pattern except that all of the buttons were covered to prevent snagging in jungle terrain.
L2494@P105-106: 103Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2495@P106: A second pattern Coat, Combat,
L2496@P106: Tropical, Wind Resistant in OG-197
L2497@P106: cotton poplin.
L2498@P106: A third pattern Coat, Combat,
L2499@P106: Tropical, Wind Resistant (Class 1),
L2500@P106: in OG-107 cotton poplin
L2501@P106: A Coat, Combat, Tropical, Wind
L2502@P106: Resistant (Class 2), in cotton ripstop.
L2503@P106: By 1967 a third pattern coat (Class 1) was standardized in either olive green shade 107, wind
L2504@P106: resistant cotton poplin or olive green shade 107, cotton rip-stop. This coat retained the slanted
L2505@P106: pockets with hidden buttons, but the shoulder loops, gas flap, and adjustment tabs were
L2506@P106: eliminated. A second pattern of this coat (Class 2) in Engineer Research and Development
L2507@P106: Laboratory (ERDL) camouflage was produced in cotton rip-stop. This uniform was issued to
L2508@P106: pathfinders, long range reconnaissance patrol members and scout/reconnaissance personnel.
L2509@P106: Each of these uniforms had matching trousers with slanted front pockets, rear pockets with flaps,
L2510@P106: and bellows-type cargo pockets with flaps on the legs.
L2511@P106: Effective July 14, 1966, the Department of the Army directed that both tapes have black lettering
L2512@P106: on an olive green shade 107 background. In 1967 rank insignia worn on the Tropical Combat
L2513@P106: Coat began being changed over to a subdued pattern of black on olive green. In 1968, all
L2514@P106: insignia, Army wide, worn on the field jacket, utility uniform and the tropical combat uniform
L2515@P106: was changed to the subdued black on olive green. In addition, the Personnel Armor System for
L2516@P106: Ground Troops (PASGT), consisting of a Kevlar helmet and a ballistic vest, was also introduced
L2517@P106: in the early 1980s. The PASGT Helmet replaced the M1 and M1C Steel Helmets for both
L2518@P106: ground troops and parachutists. The system first saw use in combat in 1983 during Operation
L2519@P106: Urgent Fury in Grenada, but most soldiers did not receive the Kevlar until a year or two later.
L2520@P106: In 1967 rank insignia worn on the Tropical Combat Coat began being changed over
L2521@P106: to a subdued pattern (black on olive green). In 1968, all insignia, Army wide, worn
L2522@P106: on the field jacket, utility uniform and the tropical combat uniform was changed to
L2523@P106: subdued. Rank insignia for enlisted personnel was moved from the sleeve to the
L2524@P106: point of the collar.
L2525@P106-107: 104Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2526@P107: 
L2527@P107: Above is a selection of insignia showing the change over from bright to subdued which began in 1967.
L2528@P107: On October 1, 1981 the Army introduced the Battle Dress Uniform or BDUs as they are called.
L2529@P107: This uniform was descended from the tropical combat uniform of the Vietnam War and consisted
L2530@P107: of a coat made of a nylon and cotton blend in woodland pattern camouflage with matching
L2531@P107: trousers, and a field cap. Because combat experience in Grenada showed that the BDU uniform
L2532@P107: was too hot for tropical climates, the Army authorized the wearing of the old tropical combat
L2533@P107: uniform for several years while adjustments were made.
L2534@P107: By 1988, a hot weather version of the BDUs in cotton rip-stop was available. The two uniforms
L2535@P107: were very similar in style, with a coat that had four straight bellows-type pockets each with a flap
L2536@P107: secured by hidden plastic buttons, and matching trousers with slanted front pockets, rear pockets
L2537@P107: with flaps, and bellows-type cargo pockets with flaps on the legs. With only minor stylistic
L2538@P107: changes such as the elimination of the waist adjustment tabs, the reduction of the size of the
L2539@P107: collar, and refinements in stitching and fit, BDUs were worn until replaced by the Army Combat
L2540@P107: Uniform in 2006.
L2541@P107: Members of the 3rd Infantry in 1987. The soldier on
L2542@P107: the left is wearing the OG-107 tropical combat
L2543@P107: uniform authorized for wear until the woodland
L2544@P107: camouflage Battle Dress Uniform as worn by the
L2545@P107: soldier on the right could be fielded.
L2546@P107: The Army also introduced a Desert Camouflage
L2547@P107: Uniform (DCU) at the same time as the woodland
L2548@P107: pattern BDU, but issue was limited to special
L2549@P107: operations troops, and soldiers assigned to
L2550@P107: exercises in the Middle East such as Operation
L2551@P107: Bright Star in Egypt. The uniform was virtually
L2552@P107: the same as the BDUs but in a six-color tan, brown
L2553@P107: and black desert camouflage pattern. Six-color
L2554@P107: DCUs have come to typify the American soldier in
L2555@P107: the Persian Gulf War (1991), although due to
L2556@P107: logistics glitch issue of the desert uniform to
L2557@P107: soldiers (especially those in VII Corps), was very
L2558@P107: restricted. The Army began issuing a new threecolor Desert Camouflage Uniform in July 1991.
L2559@P107: This uniform was worn by troop participating in
L2560@P107: Operation Enduring Freedom, and Operation Iraqi
L2561@P107: Freedom from 2002 to 2006, when it was also
L2562@P107: replaced by the Army Combat Uniform.

L2582@P108: The Army Combat Uniform (ACU) was officially established as the combat and garrison
L2583@P108: uniform for the Army on 14 June 2004, and has replaced both the Battle-Dress Uniform and the
L2584@P108: Desert Camouflage Uniform. The ACU consists of a coat, trousers, black beret or matching
L2585@P108: patrol cap, moisture wicking T-shirt, moisture wicking socks, and brown combat boots.
L2586@P108-109: 106Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2587@P109: The color scheme is composed of a gray, tan and sage green digital pattern. The color black was
L2588@P109: omitted from the uniform because it is not commonly found in nature and appears excessively
L2589@P109: dark when viewed through night vision goggles.
L2590@P109: The ACU Coat is single breasted with integrated blouse
L2591@P109: bellows for increased upper body mobility, and a plastic
L2592@P109: zipper closure that can be opened from either the top or the
L2593@P109: bottom with a front placket that covers the zipper and is
L2594@P109: secured by hook and loop (Velcro) fasteners. The coat has a
L2595@P109: Mandarin collar that can be worn up or down; tilted breast
L2596@P109: pockets with hook and loop closure; a three-slot pen pocket on
L2597@P109: the bottom of the left sleeve; and hook and loop sleeve cuff
L2598@P109: closures. On each sleeve near the shoulder there is a slanted
L2599@P109: pocket with a hook and loop covered flap closure, each with
L2600@P109: an integrated infrared identification square on the outside.
L2601@P109: Below each sleeve pocket there an elbow pouch for an
L2602@P109: internal elbow pad insert.
L2603@P109: Rank insignia is attached to a hook and loop patch located on
L2604@P109: the front center of the coat. Both the name tape and the US
L2605@P109: Army tape are attached above the left and right pockets
L2606@P109: respectively and are removable. In the future it will be much
L2607@P109: more difficult to positively identify Army uniforms since unit
L2608@P109: patches and the national identification insignia (US flag) are
L2609@P109: attached by hook and loop rather than being sewn in place.

L2649@P110: Beginning in 1982, with the introduction of the Battle Dress Uniform, the Army began
L2650@P110: manufacture of the M65 field coat in woodland pattern camouflage and desert camouflage
L2651@P110: pattern material. Subsequently, manufacture of the field coat has incorporated the changes of
L2652@P110: camouflage patterns as the have occurred, three color desert pattern in 1991 and universal pattern
L2653@P110: digital in 2005. The latest version has hook and loop patches for the attaching of the name tape,

L2655@P110: The M-1951 field cap was made of wind resistant poplin and was a slightly modified version of
L2656@P110: the original cap adopted in 1943. The M-1951 had a slightly longer visor with rows of
L2657@P110: reinforced stitching. For cold weather use, the cap had a flannel-lined fold-down flap that
L2658@P110: covered the ears and the back of the head. A number of senior officers considered the M-1951
L2659@P110: field cap to be too slovenly for a proper soldierly appearance. Unit commanders often required
L2660@P110: the cap to be worn with cardboard or various commercially available stiffeners inside, to keep it
L2661@P110: straight and upright. In 1953 this policy became official throughout the Army when Chief of
L2662@P110: Staff General Matthew B. Ridgeway began directing forces to improve their soldierly image.
L2663@P110: Commercially manufactured stiffened and blocked models of the field cap were produced and
L2664@P110: sold through the Post Exchange that met military appearance standards. The preferred model
L2665@P110: was the "Spring-Up" manufactured by Louisville Cap Corporation. These caps became
L2666@P110: universally known as “Ridgeway Caps.” While the M-1951 field cap remained standard issue,
L2667@P110: use of the Ridgeway cap became widespread throughout the 1950s.
